unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Pathogens and infectious agents as cancer drivers, illustrated by Burkitt lymphoma
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Dietary carcinogens and metabolic activation to DNA adducts, exemplified by aflatoxin
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The lecture moves from biological infectious agents to dietary and chemical carcinogens that form DNA adducts.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 7 explicitly framed infectious agents as the first entry in an overarching survey of environmental carcinogens; dietary aflatoxin simply continues that sequence.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Dietary carcinogens and aflatoxin-induced DNA adducts
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: UV radiation and the formation of thymine dimers
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The lecture transitions from chemical and dietary mutagens to physical radiation.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 10 is a brief single-paragraph example continuing the continuous inventory of environmental mutagens and mechanisms of DNA damage.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: UV radiation damage and thymine dimer formation
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Chemical carcinogens in tobacco smoke, xenobiotic metabolic activation, and tissue-specific DNA damage
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The lecture delves into detailed biochemical pathways of xenobiotic metabolism, CYP1A1 activation, and tissue specificity.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Chemical mutagens like benzo[a]pyrene and aromatic amines belong to the same broader catalog of environmental exposures causing direct DNA damage.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Chemical mutagens requiring metabolic activation to form DNA-damaging adducts
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Non-mutagenic carcinogens, tumor promoters versus initiators, and the Berenbaum two-stage carcinogenesis model
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The lecture shifts conceptually from agents that directly mutate DNA (initiators) to non-mutagenic agents that foster supportive microenvironments and proliferation (promoters), fulfilling a primary lecture learning objective.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Asbestos and chemical promoters can be seen as further examples in the ongoing survey of environmental cancer-causing agents.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Tumor promoters, chronic inflammation, and the Berenbaum two-stage model of initiation and promotion
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Host developmental timing and tissue susceptibility to carcinogenesis, followed by a section summary
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The lecture pivots from the properties of external agents to intrinsic host vulnerability and developmental life stages.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopics 16 and 17 conclude the discussion of carcinogenic mechanisms and microenvironmental context before summarizing the entire section on carcinogenesis mechanisms.

topics.label: Lecture Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer introduces herself, the cancer lecture series, and the key learning outcomes for the session.

topics.label: Fundamentals of Cancer Causation and Epidemiology
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore the biological basis of cancer as an evolutionary genetic disease influenced by intrinsic bad luck, microenvironmental factors, and population-level epidemiological variations.

topics.label: Environmental Mutagens and Direct DNA Damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail various environmental, biological, and chemical mutagens—including infectious pathogens, dietary toxins, radiation, and tobacco smoke—and the biochemical mechanisms by which they induce DNA mutations.

topics.label: Tumor Initiation, Promotion, and Host Context
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics distinguish tumor initiators from non-mutagenic promoters, examining the role of inflammation, cell signaling, and host developmental timing in cancer outgrowth.

topics.label: Methodologies for Determining Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain the experimental and analytical tools used to prove carcinogenicity, including mutational signature sequencing, biobank epidemiology, animal toxicology studies, and the Ames test.

topics.label: Conclusion and Risk-Benefit Considerations
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer concludes the session by discussing personal risk-benefit decisions regarding carcinogen exposure and summarizing the lecture's core themes.
